title: Police gun down area man; 'Great guy' shot during scuffle with cop in Edmonton
article: A former Windsor-area man who was fatally shot by Edmonton police appeared agitated before his death, telling a local newspaper that he was trying to sleep but police were outside to arrest him.
John Peter Pavic, 31, died of a gunshot wound to the chest after he allegedly ignored an officer's demand to drop a butcher knife and instead lunged at him Tuesday night.
Pavic's older sister, Maria, 36, said her brother was a great guy and police should have left him alone until he calmed down.
"Everybody was extremely shocked that happened. I thought the police could have dealt with this more carefully. Couldn't they have shot him in the leg or something?"' she said.
John was one of six children raised by Peter and Yaga Pavic. His mother died of breast cancer 10 years ago.
"It would be nice to get our story out but we've been instructed not to speak to the media," said a man who answered the phone at a Pavic residence in Maidstone.
In his call to the Edmonton Journal prior to his death, Pavic declined to say why police wanted to arrest him.
He said he had phoned them previously.
"I'm not going to let them in because they don't have a search warrant," he said.

Pavic said he had earlier called a lawyer and he wanted media present to cover the incident. "I'm a pretty good guy," he said. "I didn't do nothing wrong. It's the cops, they've got guns." He said police had phoned him three times but he had hung up on them.

Stephen Jenuth, a Calgary lawyer and president of the Alberta Civil Liberties Association, said the best option would have been for officers to wait until Pavic was calm enough to come out on his own.
"It should mean backing off, talking and sending in the next shift of officers."
But Edmonton police Chief Bob Wasylyshen said Thursday the officer who fired the fatal shots was in a life and death struggle with a drunken armed man.
After deploying his taser, which he believed had made proper contact, four tactical members entered the suite.
The gun-shaped taser weapons are designed to stop people cold by sending 60,000 volts through their central nervous system.

A taser fires two tiny darts attached to a wire. Once they stick to a person's skin or clothing, they emit a charge that freezes the body and often causes the person to fall. Both darts must make contact for the taser to work.
The lead officer was attacked at the top of a flight of stairs by Pavic who was armed with a butcher knife, the chief said. An inquiry will be held into Pavic's death.
